tagline: Along Alameda Creek, two railway lines share a narrow canyon.
intro: Niles Canyon Road follows Alameda Creek’s canyon between Fremont’s Niles district and Sunol. Parts of the valley are extremely narrow. Caltrans designates Route 84 from Route 238 to I-680 as a scenic highway, under criteria calling for a “memorable landscape” without “visual intrusions.” The road connects Sunol and Fremont in seven miles, alongside both a heritage railway and an active Union Pacific mainline.

Before the highway, the overland route El Camino Viejo a Los Ángeles passed through the canyon. In September 1869, the first through train from Sacramento reached Alameda Terminal through this passage. The line lost its transcontinental traffic to a shorter Benicia route in 1879. By around 1900, Niles attracted picnic day-trippers, and the name Niles Canyon replaced the earlier Alameda Cañon. A later Western Pacific line, built through the canyon in 1905–1908, required two tunnels and a steel bridge.

Begin at Niles, where the Vallejo Flour Mill ruins mark the canyon’s western end, then follow the creek toward Sunol. The former Southern Pacific alignment follows the north side, now used by the Niles Canyon Railway; the newer Union Pacific line lies to the south. Sunol lies near Alameda Creek at the northwest edge of the Sunol Valley.

moments.title: Niles
moments.text: Essanay’s Niles studio began in an empty barn in 1912. The following year the company built ten cottages for actors and a studio near the railroad tracks. More than 350 Essanay films were made here, and Charlie Chaplin filmed The Tramp in the canyon. Chaplin later moved his production unit to Los Angeles, disliking Niles’s chilly climate and Chicago’s unpredictable weather. The lot closed in 1916 and was demolished by the 1930s. The Niles Essanay Silent Film Museum occupies the Edison Theater, half a block from the former studio site, preserving silent films and motion-picture equipment.

moments.title: Vallejo Flour Mill
moments.text: A stone foundation survives from the second Vallejo Flour Mill, built in 1856 at the mouth of the canyon. José de Jesús Vallejo built the first mill in 1841, with a dam and aqueduct to provide power. A watercolor from 1856 by Vallejo’s daughter Carmelita depicts the three-story mill and its large wooden wheel. Rail construction later displaced the waterworks: Vallejo’s aqueduct was torn out for the new line and rebuilt. In 1909, Southern Pacific demolished the original adobe mill to make room for a railway junction. The ruins occupy Vallejo Mill Historical Park at Niles Canyon Road and Mission Boulevard.
moments.notice: The surviving stone foundation belongs to the second mill, built in 1856.

moments.title: Niles Canyon Railway
moments.text: Chinese laborers built the railway bed into the canyon’s tight curves and narrow banks during the 1860s. Their work included masonry culverts, retaining walls and bridge piers as well as wooden bridges. Much of that stonework remains visible. Steel bridges replaced covered wooden spans at Farwell and Dresser, while original cut-stone abutments, culverts and retaining walls survived later rebuilding. After Southern Pacific ended operations in 1984, the Pacific Locomotive Association began rebuilding track in 1987. Its first passenger train left Sunol in May 1988. The heritage railway now uses both steam and diesel locomotives for public excursions.

moments.title: Sunol
moments.text: Sunol’s 1884 depot combined passenger, freight and railway-agent facilities under one roof. It is the last survivor of at least eleven Southern Pacific No. 7 depots. The agent’s office has a five-window bay on the track side and a small ticket window opening into the passenger waiting room. The freight-room floor was raised to match freight cars and teamsters’ wagons. That room now holds exhibits and meetings, while the building retains the arrangement that once brought several kinds of railroad business together. A gable roof covers the east end; an elevated hip roof marks the freight room at the west.
